1. Core Clinical Tension: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 3-month history of sporadic gingivorrhagia and worsening epistaxis accompanied by high fever (39.5°C), acute respiratory distress, severe wasting (weight-for-height -2 SD), massive splenomegaly (Hackett grade IV, 12 cm), hepatomegaly (11 cm), and profound cytopenias (hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL, platelets 3,000/mm³). Because this child lived in an urban suburb without travel history to classical endemic foci, the combination of hepatosplenomegaly, generalized adenopathy, and life-threatening bicytopenia strongly mimicked acute hematologic malignancy (such as acute lymphoblastic or myeloid leukemia) or severe tropical infections (such as malaria or sepsis).

2. Admission Breakpoint: Evaluation concludes after the initial clinical examination, triage vital signs, anthropometrics, emergency laboratory testing (severe anemia, profound thrombocytopenia, peripheral blood smear showing 7% blasts and 3% erythroblasts, capillary glucose 1.3 g/L), admission chest radiography (bilateral pneumonia), and abdominal ultrasound (confirming hepatosplenomegaly), strictly prior to lymph node histopathology, invasive bone marrow aspirate Giemsa staining, and targeted species-specific molecular PCR assays.

3. Differential Distinctions: Malignant hematologic disease (acute leukemia) is ruled out by bone marrow cytology showing lack of blast predominance and presence of intracellular protozoan forms. Endemic protozoal infections (malaria), viral hepatitis, HIV/retroviral infection, hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease), and nutritional cytopenias (vitamin B9/B12 deficiency) are systematically ruled out by standard clinical, serological, and hematologic workups.
case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric emergency department of a tertiary teaching hospital in Senegal due to worsening epistaxis and bleeding gums that had been occurring sporadically over the preceding 3 months without formal medical follow-up. The patient resided in an urban suburban district characterized by stagnant water, swampy areas, and roaming domestic animals. All family members regularly slept under insecticide-treated bed nets, and the child had no history of travel outside his residential municipality. His parents and 13-month-old sibling were reported to be healthy.

On physical examination, the child was acutely ill and febrile. Vital signs revealed a body temperature of 39.5°C, heart rate of 153 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 48 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 93/62 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 97% on ambient air. Anthropometric measurements indicated nutritional wasting: weight was 12 kg and height was 97 cm (weight-for-height ratio at -2 standard deviations), with a mid-upper arm circumference of 13 cm. Examination revealed prominent hemorrhagic manifestations, including profuse bilateral epistaxis with blood clots, gingival bleeding, and multiple oral mucosal ulcers. He exhibited clinical signs of severe poorly tolerated anemia and moderate respiratory distress. Abdominal examination demonstrated marked organomegaly with hepatomegaly extending 11 cm and massive splenomegaly extending 12 cm below the costal margin (Hackett classification grade IV). Palpation of lymph nodes revealed generalized, non-inflammatory macro-polyadenopathy in the cervical and axillary regions. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Immediate bedside and baseline laboratory investigations showed a capillary blood glucose of 1.3 g/L. The complete blood count demonstrated severe hypochromic microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 5.1 g/dL, severe thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 3,000/mm³, and leukocytosis. Peripheral blood smear examination demonstrated 7% blasts and 3% erythroblasts, which did not fulfill diagnostic criteria for blast crisis. A plain chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates consistent with bilateral pneumonia. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed marked hepatomegaly and splenomegaly with homogeneous echotexture and no focal lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The dramatic triad of massive hepatosplenomegaly, generalized macropolyadenopathy, and life-threatening cytopenias (hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL, platelets 3,000/mm³) raised high suspicion for leukemia, but the peripheral smear demonstrated only 7% blasts and 3% erythroblasts, which was inconsistent with an acute blast crisis.
